metadata.description: Reference info for the 8 monkey species in the classifier. Keys match the folder / class names used in training.
metadata.note: IUCN statuses can change when species are reassessed; re-check at iucnredlist.org before publishing.

Semnopithecus entellus.range: Northern and central India (lowlands north of the Godavari and Krishna rivers, south of the Ganges); also parts of Nepal, Bangladesh and Pakistan
Semnopithecus entellus.habitat: Dry deciduous forest, scrub, plains and human-dominated areas including towns and temples
Semnopithecus entellus.diet: Mostly leaves (folivore), plus fruit and flowers
identifying_features: Silver-gray coat with a yellowish tinge
Black face, ears, hands and feet
Semnopithecus entellus.fun_fact: Sacred in Hinduism and named after the god Hanuman, so it is often tolerated or fed around temples.

Macaca mulatta.range: Widespread across South, Central and Southeast Asia, including India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand and China
Macaca mulatta.habitat: Forests, scrub, farmland, towns and cities; very adaptable
Macaca mulatta.diet: Omnivore: fruit, seeds, leaves, insects, and human food
identifying_features: Brown to grayish-brown fur, paler on the underside
Medium-length tail, shorter than a bonnet macaque's
Macaca mulatta.fun_fact: One of the most studied primates in biomedical research; the Rh blood factor is named after it.

Macaca radiata.habitat: Dry and moist forests, forest edges, farmland, towns and temples
Macaca radiata.diet: Omnivore: fruit, leaves, insects, eggs, small reptiles, and human food
identifying_features: Whorl of hair on the crown that is parted in the middle, like a cap or bonnet
Bald forehead and sides of the head
Gray-brown to golden-brown coat, darker on the back
Macaca radiata.fun_fact: Two subspecies are recognized: dark-bellied and pale-bellied. Habitat loss and human-monkey conflict are the main threats.

Macaca silenus.range: Endemic to the Western Ghats of southern India (Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu)
Macaca silenus.habitat: Tropical evergreen rainforest, mostly in the canopy
Macaca silenus.diet: Mostly fruit and seeds, plus insects and other small animals
identifying_features: Tufted tail tip like a lion's
Macaca silenus.fun_fact: Depends heavily on intact rainforest, so it is highly sensitive to forest fragmentation.

Semnopithecus johnii.range: Endemic to the southern Western Ghats (Nilgiri, Palani, Anamalai and Cardamom hills) in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu
Semnopithecus johnii.habitat: Montane shola forests and evergreen forests, plus plantations
Semnopithecus johnii.diet: Mostly leaves (folivore), plus fruit, seeds and flowers
Semnopithecus johnii.fun_fact: Sometimes still listed under the older name Trachypithecus johnii in older books and websites.

Trachypithecus geei.range: Western Assam in India and adjoining southern Bhutan, in a small area of forest between the Sankosh and Manas rivers
Trachypithecus geei.habitat: Subtropical and tropical forest, including forest fragments
Trachypithecus geei.diet: Mostly leaves (folivore), plus fruit, flowers and seeds
identifying_features: Cream to golden-chestnut coat, which varies with season
Trachypithecus geei.fun_fact: Named after the naturalist E. P. Gee, who brought it to scientific attention in the 1950s.

Macaca munzala.range: Western Arunachal Pradesh, India (Tawang and West Kameng districts); sightings reported in nearby Bhutan and Tibet
Macaca munzala.habitat: High-altitude forests, often close to villages and farmland
Macaca munzala.diet: Omnivore: fruit, leaves, insects and crops
Macaca munzala.fun_fact: Described as a new species only in 2005.

Macaca arctoides.range: Northeast India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Vietnam, southern China and northern peninsular Malaysia
Macaca arctoides.habitat: Tropical and subtropical evergreen forest, from lowlands to hills
Macaca arctoides.diet: Mostly fruit, plus leaves, seeds and small animals
identifying_features: Bare face that turns red and darkens with age
Macaca arctoides.fun_fact: Adults are often almost hairless on the crown, which gives the face a bald look.
